beginner_glossary.IDM (Integrated Device Manufacturer): A company that BOTH designs chips and makes them in its own factories — unlike 'fabless' designers (e.g., NVIDIA) who outsource making, or 'foundries' (e.g., TSMC) who only make. Intel is the classic IDM, now also trying to be a foundry for others.
beginner_glossary.Foundry (Intel Foundry): A business that manufactures chips to other companies' designs. Intel Foundry is Intel's contract-manufacturing arm — currently loss-making (about $10B in 2025) as it builds leading-edge nodes and seeks external customers.
beginner_glossary.Fabless: A chip company that designs but doesn't manufacture (e.g., NVIDIA, AMD). Relevant because Intel wants fabless companies to become its foundry customers.
beginner_glossary.x86: The decades-old processor instruction set that powers most PCs and servers. Intel and AMD are the two big x86 makers; ARM is the main alternative architecture.
beginner_glossary.Xeon: Intel's brand of server (data-center) CPUs. Xeon demand is central to Intel's AI thesis — that CPUs are essential alongside GPUs.
beginner_glossary.CCG / DCAI / Intel Foundry / All Other: Intel's reporting segments. CCG (Client Computing Group) = PC chips; DCAI (Data Center & AI) = server CPUs and AI/ASIC; Intel Foundry = contract manufacturing; All Other = Mobileye (self-driving) and Altera (FPGAs).
beginner_glossary.Process node (Intel 7 / 4 / 3 / 18A / 14: Generations of Intel's chip-making technology, newer = more advanced. Intel 18A ('1.8nm-class') is its leading node now ramping; Intel 14A is the next one (its maturity is reportedly outpacing 18A at the same stage). Naming differs from TSMC's (N3/N2).
beginner_glossary.18A / Panther Lake: Intel 18A is the new leading-edge node; 'Panther Lake' (Core Ultra Series 3) is the first big PC product built on it. Early-ramp 18A has low yields and below-average margins, so it is a near-term gross-margin headwind even as volume grows fast.
beginner_glossary.EUV (Extreme Ultraviolet lithography): The most advanced chip-printing tool (from ASML), required for leading-edge nodes like Intel 3/18A/14A.
beginner_glossary.Advanced packaging (Foveros / EMIB): Stitching multiple chips into one package — a key value-add and a growth area for Intel Foundry, with backlog reportedly in the billions of dollars per year. Intel's EMIB is a substrate-based approach (an alternative to TSMC's CoWoS).
beginner_glossary.AIPC (AI PC): A PC with a built-in AI accelerator (NPU). Intel's Core Ultra chips target this; AIPC is now >60% of Intel's client CPU mix.
beginner_glossary.Granite Rapids / Diamond Rapids / Coral: Intel's server-CPU roadmap. Coral Rapids will add 'simultaneous multithreading' (SMT) to compete better with AMD.
beginner_glossary.ASIC / XPU: ASIC = a custom chip built for one customer's specific workload; XPU = Intel's term for its mix of CPU/GPU/accelerator silicon. Intel's ASIC business is already a >$1B run-rate and growing.
beginner_glossary.Host CPU: The CPU that manages an AI server full of GPUs (orchestration, security, networking). Xeon 6 was chosen as the host CPU for NVIDIA's DGX Rubin systems.
beginner_glossary.CPU-to-GPU ratio: How many GPUs are paired with each CPU in AI servers. Training used ~7-8 GPUs per CPU; inference ~3-4; agentic AI may move toward parity — meaning MORE CPUs per system, Intel's core bull thesis.
beginner_glossary.Agentic AI / physical AI: Next-stage AI that plans and acts (agents), and AI in robots/edge devices. Intel argues these are CPU-heavy workloads.
beginner_glossary.TeraFab: A new partnership Intel announced with Elon Musk's SpaceX, xAI, and Tesla to explore unconventional ways to improve chip-manufacturing economics — early-stage and strategic.
beginner_glossary.Fab 34 (Ireland): An Intel fab in Ireland; in 2026 Intel bought back the 49% it didn't own (a joint-investment stake) for ~$7.7B cash + $6.5B new debt, to capture full economics.
beginner_glossary.Foundry operating loss: The money Intel Foundry loses each period. It was about $10.3B in 2025 (on $17.8B sales) — the single biggest drag on Intel's overall profitability; it should narrow as 18A yields improve.
beginner_glossary.GAAP vs non-GAAP: GAAP = official accounting (includes everything). Non-GAAP = company-adjusted (strips some items). Intel is modestly profitable on non-GAAP but loss-making on GAAP — always check which one a figure uses.
beginner_glossary.Forward P/E: Share price divided by NEXT year's expected earnings. Intel has no trailing P/E (it's losing money on GAAP); its forward P/E is ~118x, very high, meaning the price assumes a big earnings recovery.
beginner_glossary.U.S. government stake / NVIDIA & SoftBan: In 2025 the U.S. government took a ~10% Intel stake ($8.9B), and NVIDIA ($5B) and SoftBank ($2B) invested — strengthening the balance sheet and signaling strategic/national importance, but adding political and governance complexity.

company_snapshot.what_it_is: Intel is the iconic American chipmaker — an IDM that designs and manufactures CPUs for PCs and servers, and is now also building a contract foundry to make chips for others. It is in the middle of a high-stakes turnaround under CEO Lip-Bu Tan: rebuilding leading-edge manufacturing (Intel 18A/14A), leaning into a thesis that CPUs are indispensable in the AI era, and trying to turn its ~$10B/year-loss foundry into a viable business — backed by a ~10% U.S. government stake plus NVIDIA and SoftBank investments.
company_snapshot.founder_ceo: Founded by Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore. CEO: Lip-Bu Tan (since early 2025). CFO: David Zinsner.
company_snapshot.manufacturing_footprint: Owns a vast global fab network — Arizona, Oregon, New Mexico, Ohio (under construction) in the U.S., plus Ireland (Fab 34, now fully owned), Israel, and others; advanced packaging incl. a multiyear expansion in Malaysia. Unusually for a chip designer, Intel makes most of its own chips and also uses TSMC for some products (a multi-foundry approach). [Q1 2026 call, 2026-04-23]

business_model.summary: Intel makes money two ways. (1) PRODUCTS: designing and selling CPUs and chips for PCs (CCG) and data centers (DCAI), plus Mobileye/Altera — these segments are profitable. (2) MANUFACTURING/FOUNDRY: running its fabs, increasingly for external customers — currently deeply loss-making as it ramps leading-edge nodes (18A/14A). The whole-company result is roughly breakeven because product profits are largely offset by ~$10B/year of foundry losses. The turnaround thesis: AI is reviving CPU demand (Xeon), 18A/14A fix the manufacturing gap, and the foundry eventually breaks even and grows — supported by U.S. government and strategic-investor backing.
how_they_make_money: Client Computing (CCG): PC CPUs (Core Ultra/Core Series), incl. AI PCs. Q1 2026 revenue $7.7B, operating profit $2.5B (33% margin). [Q1 2026 call]
Data Center & AI (DCAI): Xeon server CPUs and a fast-growing custom-ASIC business (>$1B run-rate). Q1 2026 revenue $5.1B (+22% YoY), operating profit $1.5B (31%). [Q1 2026 call]
Intel Foundry: contract manufacturing + advanced packaging. Q1 2026 revenue $5.4B (mostly internal; external only $174M) but an operating LOSS of $2.4B. [Q1 2026 call]
All Other (Mobileye + Altera): Q1 2026 revenue $628M, operating profit $102M. [Q1 2026 call]
competitive_moat_analyst_view: x86 CPU franchise: a huge installed base in PCs and servers, now positioned as the 'orchestration layer' of AI systems as CPU-to-GPU ratios move back toward CPUs. [Q1 2026 call]

Owned manufacturing + advanced packaging: a vast fab network and packaging (EMIB/Foveros) give supply control and a foundry option few rivals have — a differentiator as leading-edge wafers stay scarce. [Q1 2026 call]
National-champion backing: a ~10% U.S. government stake plus NVIDIA and SoftBank investments strengthen the balance sheet and signal strategic importance (with strings attached). [2025 filings]
Turnaround momentum: six straight quarters of beating guidance, 18A running ahead of plan, and AI-CPU demand outpacing supply — early evidence the rebuild is working. [Q1 2026 call]
facts: Q1 2026: revenue $13.6B (+7% YoY, $1.4B above midpoint), non-GAAP gross margin 41%, non-GAAP EPS $0.29 (incl. ~$0.06 one-time gain); AI-driven businesses now 60% of revenue, +40% YoY. [Q1 2026 call, 2026-04-23]
FY2025: revenue $52.9B (flat), GAAP net loss $267M; Intel Foundry operating loss $10.318B on $17.826B sales (vs a $2.249B foundry loss in 2024). [FY2025 results, 2026-01]
Demand exceeds supply across all businesses; Intel says it is undershipping demand by an amount that 'starts with a b' (billions). [Q1 2026 call]
assumptions: ASSUMPTION: the CPU-revival thesis is durable (agentic AI keeps lifting CPU content per system), sustaining Xeon growth into 2027 and beyond.
ASSUMPTION: 18A/14A yields keep improving and Intel Foundry wins enough external customers to narrow and eventually erase its ~$10B/year loss.

revenue_streams.analyst_view: The product engines (CCG + DCAI) are genuinely profitable and DCAI is inflecting on the AI-CPU thesis (Xeon + ASIC). The problem is Intel Foundry: it generates big revenue but mostly from Intel itself, books almost no external revenue yet ($174M), and loses ~$10B/year. So the investment debate is really 'product turnaround that's working' vs 'foundry that must stop bleeding' — and the stock now prices in BOTH going right.

competitors.landscape_summary: Intel competes on three fronts: server/PC CPUs (vs AMD and the ARM ecosystem), AI accelerators (vs NVIDIA/AMD, where Intel is small), and foundry (vs TSMC and Samsung, where Intel is a distant, loss-making challenger). Notably, NVIDIA is simultaneously a rival (accelerators), a customer (host CPUs), AND an investor — a sign of how entangled the AI supply chain has become.

key_competitors.note: Intel's direct x86 rival in PC and server CPUs (EPYC), and a strong AI-GPU challenger (Instinct). Has taken server-CPU share from Intel for years; Intel's roadmap (Diamond/Coral Rapids, SMT) aims to fight back.
Dominant AI-accelerator maker — a competitor where Intel is small, but ALSO a customer (Xeon 6 hosts DGX Rubin) and a $5B investor. Both rival and partner. (See reports/NVIDIA.json.)

key_competitors.company: ARM ecosystem (Arm, Ampere, AWS Graviton, Google Axion, NVIDIA CPUs)
key_competitors.note: ARM-based server CPUs are the longer-term architectural threat to x86; hyperscalers build their own (Graviton, Axion). Intel must defend x86's role.

The dominant foundry Intel is trying to catch (and also uses as a supplier). Intel positions 18A/14A as a leading-edge alternative; the gap in scale/yield/customers is still large. (See reports/TSMC.json.)
The other would-be leading-edge foundry; competes with Intel for the #2/#3 foundry position behind TSMC. (See reports/Samsung.json.)

competitors.differentiation_analyst_view: Intel's distinctive pitch is being the only Western company with leading-edge CPU design AND owned leading-edge manufacturing AND advanced packaging — plus government/strategic backing. Its weaknesses are equally clear: it trails AMD in CPU competitiveness in places, is a minor player in AI accelerators (NVIDIA's domain), and its foundry is far behind TSMC and losing ~$10B/year. The bull case needs the CPU revival AND a foundry turnaround; the bear case is that it stays a competitive-but-second product company saddled with a cash-burning foundry.
facts: Xeon 6 was selected as the host CPU for NVIDIA's DGX Rubin NVL8 systems — evidence Intel CPUs remain central even in NVIDIA-led AI servers. [Q1 2026 call, 2026-04-23]

financial_performance.analyst_view: The operational trajectory is genuinely better: six straight beats, 41% non-GAAP gross margin, AI-CPU demand outstripping supply, 18A ahead of plan, and a narrowing (but still huge) foundry loss. But the honest financial picture is that Intel is STILL GAAP-loss-making on a trailing basis (-$3.17B), the foundry lost ~$10B in 2025, and free cash flow is negative. The investment case hinges on the foundry loss shrinking fast and the CPU revival compounding — neither yet proven in the GAAP numbers.

implied_multiples_analyst_view.interpretation: This is one of the most extended valuations among large-cap semis relative to current profits: a ~6-7x one-year run to ~$626B market cap on a company that is GAAP-unprofitable and whose foundry loses ~$10B/year. The price embeds (a) the CPU-revival thesis playing out, (b) the foundry turning around, and (c) the value of government/strategic backing. If those materialize, today's price can be grown into on 2027-2028 earnings; if any slips, the downside is large.

valuation.analyst_view: Valuation is the crux of the Intel story and the clearest caution flag. The operational comeback is real, but the share price (up ~6-7x in a year, ~118x forward earnings, ~11.6x sales) has run far ahead of the GAAP financials AND ahead of Wall Street: analysts are at HOLD with an average target ~25% below the current price. In other words, the market has already priced in a successful turnaround that the income statement has not yet delivered. The debate is not whether Intel is improving (it is) but whether the improvement justifies a ~$626B valuation on a still-loss-making, foundry-burdened company.

risks.risk: Valuation far ahead of profits (and of analysts)
risks.why_it_matters: Up ~6-7x in a year to ~$626B / ~118x forward earnings / ~11.6x sales while GAAP-unprofitable — and trading ~25% ABOVE the average analyst target ($93). The price embeds a turnaround not yet in the numbers; downside is large if it disappoints (52-week low $18.97).
Intel Foundry lost $10.3B in 2025 with almost no external revenue ($174M in Q1); the whole thesis needs this to narrow sharply and win outside customers.
Leading-edge ramps are hard; 18A is still a gross-margin headwind and below corporate-average margins. Slips would delay the foundry turnaround and product margins.
AMD keeps pressing in x86; ARM-based server CPUs (Graviton/Axion/NVIDIA) threaten x86 long-term; NVIDIA dominates accelerators where Intel is small.

risks.risk: Still GAAP-unprofitable / negative free cash flow
risks.why_it_matters: Trailing GAAP net loss -$3.17B and Q1 adjusted FCF -$2B; the comeback is not yet visible in official earnings or cash generation.
Full-year PC unit TAM guided down low-double-digit %, pressuring Intel's largest (CCG) segment in 2H.
Rising memory, wafer, substrate, and glass-substrate costs are 2H gross-margin headwinds management explicitly flagged.
A ~10% U.S. government stake plus NVIDIA/SoftBank ownership adds political, governance, and conflict-of-interest considerations to capital allocation and strategy.
Tens of billions in CapEx plus the debt-funded Fab 34 buyout strain cash while earnings are depressed.
The 2025 equity raises (government/NVIDIA/SoftBank) added shares; further capital needs could dilute holders more.

final_research_summary.one_paragraph: Intel (INTC) is the iconic American chipmaker in the middle of a high-stakes turnaround under CEO Lip-Bu Tan. It is an IDM (designs and manufactures CPUs for PCs and servers) that is also building a contract foundry — and is unusually backed by a ~10% U.S. government stake plus NVIDIA ($5B) and SoftBank ($2B) investments made in 2025. Operationally, the comeback is real: Q1 2026 (reported 2026-04-23) was the SIXTH straight beat — revenue $13.6B (+7% YoY), non-GAAP gross margin 41%, non-GAAP EPS $0.29 — with AI-driven businesses now 60% of revenue (+40% YoY), Xeon server demand outpacing supply, and the new Intel 18A node running ahead of plan. The core thesis is that the CPU is 're-inserting' itself in the AI era (the CPU-to-GPU ratio moving from ~1:8 toward parity as AI turns agentic). BUT the financial reality is sobering: on a GAAP basis Intel is still LOSS-MAKING on a trailing basis (-$3.17B), FY2025 was roughly breakeven (revenue $52.9B flat, net loss $267M), and Intel Foundry lost a staggering $10.3B in 2025 with almost no external revenue. Meanwhile the stock has run ~6-7x in a year (from $18.97 to ~$124.57, an all-time high) to a ~$626B market cap — ~118x FORWARD earnings and ~11.6x sales — and now trades ~25% ABOVE the average analyst target of $93 (consensus rating: HOLD). So what is FACT is a genuine, government-backed operational turnaround with improving products and an AI-CPU tailwind; what is being PRICED is the FULL success of that turnaround AND a foundry that still loses ~$10B/year. The central debate is not whether Intel is improving — it is — but whether a still-unprofitable, foundry-burdened company justifies a ~$626B valuation that has already outrun both its own income statement and Wall Street's targets.
